policy.//: A date moves ONLY on a RETRIEVAL EVENT. Never because time passed. Never because a document was written. Reading a term does not install it; only retrieving it does.
policy.//2: Expanding ladder for a repeatedly-passed atom: 14d → 30d → 60d → 120d. A FAILED cold re-check resets to 1 and DEMOTES the atom.
policy.//3: LOST/MISUSED = drill EVERY session until produced COLD. Repair a LOST term by RE-DERIVING the mechanism and RE-CHRISTENING it (name-at-birth) — never by quizzing it harder. TEACHING_LOG Entry 004.
policy.promotion: A term goes → COLD only when produced cold in a LATER session than the one that taught it. A same-session production proves working memory and promotes NOTHING.
policy.demotion: Any atom whose TERMS fail a cold check is demoted to `termslost`, regardless of how well the mechanism was explained. CLAUDE.md §1.

build.//: The build tier obeys the same law as the atoms: what he DERIVES survives, what he is HANDED rots. That law does not stop applying because the artifact is a repo instead of a word.
build.labIsNotAGate: A lab makes a mechanism VISIBLE. It does not bank an atom. Only a cold gate does.
build.boundaryOpens: A boundary may leave `locked` ONLY when every required atom is `banked`. You cannot build on an atom you have not banked — you would be pasting, not deriving.
build.guidedRule: GUIDED = Jimmy is architect + reviewer. Hema types 100% of the code. When he is stuck, Jimmy asks a question that unblocks him — Jimmy NEVER hands him the answer. A project Jimmy wrote teaches Hema nothing and puts a lie on his LinkedIn.
build.soloIsTheGate: The SOLO project IS the mastery gate for the boundary — it covers gate parts 2 (applied), 4 (new scenario) and 5 (failure+recovery), because code that runs cannot be hedged at, echoed back, or answered around. Jimmy writes the problem statement and does not touch the build. The oral gate still covers parts 1 (explain), 3 (tradeoff) and 6 (terms).
build.articleGate: An article may be published ONLY after the solo project is `gated`. Never before. Publishing half-known material under his own name is a debt that compounds in public. The article ships per PROJECT, never per day.
build.everyProjectShips: Requirements · API · schema · failure injection · monitoring · a README a stranger can run. 'It works on my machine' is not shipped.
build.atomBuild: ATOM BUILD: some atoms support a standalone real project on their own — they do NOT wait for the boundary. (Hema's correction, S8, and he was right: making him wait 9 atoms to build anything was a smaller copy of 'builds start after Module 2'.) Bar: it must DEMYSTIFY A BLACK BOX HE ALREADY DEPENDS ON. Build the resolver, not an app that calls DNS. Build the load balancer, not an app that is load balanced. He should finish unable to be mystified by the production version again. Same law as everything else: HE TYPES EVERY LINE.
build.deploymentRule: ★ LOCALHOST IS A TOY. (Hema's ask, S8, and it is the right instinct.) Every build ships to the REAL INTERNET: a domain he actually owns, a public IP, and a real TLS certificate. A DNS resolver on localhost is a toy; a DNS resolver answering real queries for a domain he owns is engineering — and it makes atoms 1.3, 1.9, 1.15 and 1.16 PHYSICAL instead of theoretical. Prefer free/cheap tiers, but a ~$10/yr domain is worth it and is the single highest-leverage purchase in this curriculum. NEVER quote him cloud pricing from memory — free tiers change (AWS's changed in 2025). CHECK, then tell him the cost before he clicks anything.
build.threeTiers: LAB (every atom, 20-30min, SEE it) → ATOM BUILD (some atoms, a real deployed thing) → BOUNDARY PROJECT (guided, then SOLO = the gate) → ARTICLE (after the solo gates).

primitives.//: TEACHING_LOG Entry 010. STATUS.json tracked what he ANSWERED and never what he was GIVEN — so 'he could not derive it' and 'nobody ever taught him the primitive' looked IDENTICAL in the record, and they need opposite responses. S9 asked him to derive asymmetric signatures. Rivest, Shamir and Adleman took months. He is not going to do it between two messages.
primitives.rule: Jimmy may ONLY ask him to derive from a primitive listed in the atom's `given`. If the needed primitive is in `lacks`, the question is ILLEGAL.

derive.yes: Derivable from `given`. Ask. Do not tell. (fast retransmit from cumulative ACKs — he did exactly this, cold, unaided.)
derive.need-only: The MECHANISM must be HANDED — nobody derives it in a session. But the NEED for it is derivable, and that is what you derive. Shape: pose the requirement → he confirms his current tools cannot meet it → hand the tool → HE applies it. He derives WHY it must exist; he is handed WHAT it is. (signatures, DH, consistent hashing, Paxos, B-trees.)
derive.no: Hand it. Vocabulary, conventions, port numbers, RFC facts. There is nothing to derive and pretending otherwise wastes his session.

primitives.//2: 'What he is HANDED rots' (BEHAVIOR_LEARNING, the governing law) is TRUE and it created this bug: every Jimmy who met an underivable primitive tried to interrogate it out of him rather than admit it must be given. The method ate its own exception. Handing is not the failure. Handing WITHOUT deriving the need is the failure.

modules.name: Networking
modules.broke: Two computers. No shared memory. The only way to know anything about another machine is to send a message and wait — and the message may never arrive. Every single thing in distributed systems is a consequence of that one fact.
modules.buys: A name resolves to an address (DNS). An address becomes a reliable ordered byte pipe (TCP). The pipe becomes private and authenticated (TLS). The tunnel carries a request and gets a response (HTTP). That is the whole internet, and you can now walk it end to end.
modules.costs: Reliability is bought with latency — that is head-of-line blocking, and it is why UDP exists, why HTTP/2 did not fix what it claimed to, and why QUIC was built. And the wire gives you one machine. The moment there are ten of them: where does the truth live? That question is a database.

atoms.t: OSI (7 layers) vs the real TCP/IP model (4 layers)
atoms.trap: The internet is 4 layers. OSI's 7 are a teaching artifact you must be able to NAME but will rarely use.

lab.see: ONE packet, four headers wrapped around each other: Ethernet | IP | TCP | HTTP. Peel the onion by hand. That IS the 4-layer model — not a diagram, an actual byte layout.
Per-hop packet loss on a real path. Packets vanish and NOBODY retransmits, nobody apologises, nobody even knows. That is best-effort, and you are looking at it.

atoms.real: A packet from your laptop to Google crosses ~12 routers, and NOT ONE of them promised to deliver it. Run `mtr -rwc 100 1.1.1.1` and watch loss at an intermediate hop while the destination stays at 0% — that hop is deprioritising ICMP, not dropping your data. Best-effort is not a metaphor.

atoms.t: DNS — recursive resolver · root → TLD → authoritative · TTL · stale · trust anchor
atoms.ref: ⭐ Implement DNS in a Weekend (you build a resolver)

lab.cmd: dig +trace google.com  ·  then: dig google.com  (twice, 5s apart)
lab.see: root → TLD → authoritative, one hop at a time, on your screen. Then watch the TTL COUNT DOWN in the cache on the second dig. Stale is a number, ticking.

build.name: A real DNS resolver, from scratch
build.what: Not a wrapper around getaddrinfo — a resolver that speaks the DNS wire format, starts at the ROOT HINTS, and walks root → TLD → authoritative itself. Then caches, and honours TTL.
build.why: This is literally the reference already in his syllabus (*Implement DNS in a Weekend*) and it was never assigned. He walks the chain in code that he wrote.
build.real: Point his OWN domain at it. Serve real queries. `dig @his-server his-domain.dev` from another machine and get an answer back.
build.note: S8 2026-07-14: encodeName ✓ (length-prefixed labels + zero terminator), buildHeader ✓ (12 bytes, 6 uint16 slots, random ID), buildQuery ✓ (type=A class=IN), UDP send ✓ — GOT A REAL 488-BYTE REFERRAL FROM a.root-servers.net. Decoded the response header cold: NSCOUNT=13, ARCOUNT=11 matched the first dig. STOPPED at the parsing wall: skip header+question, then read records — and DNS NAME COMPRESSION (0xc0 pointer) is the boss fight. Resume: where does the question section end → then parse RRs → then the referral-follow loop.

atoms.real: Oct 2016: the Dyn DDoS took out Twitter, Reddit, Netflix and GitHub for most of the US east coast. None of those servers went down. Only the thing that TRANSLATES THEIR NAMES did. He is currently building the resolver that would have been affected.

atoms.t: TCP — the 3-way handshake. Purpose: sync sequence numbers BOTH directions; liveness is a side-effect

lab.see: SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK with the REAL initial sequence numbers — and you'll see there are TWO of them, one per direction. That is what the handshake is FOR.

atoms.real: SYN floods: an attacker sends SYN and never completes the handshake, so the server holds half-open state until it runs out. The defence (SYN cookies) exists because the 3-way handshake forces the server to remember something before the client has proven it is real.

atoms.t: TCP loss recovery — flowing → fast retransmit (3 dup-ACKs) · silent → RTO + exponential backoff
atoms.trap: Mechanism re-derived COLD in S5 — but he could name none of it. Under the gate rule (description without the term is not a pass) this is NOT banked. Re-gate due.
atoms.note: MECHANISM re-derived cold S5, unaided. TERMS: none produced. Demoted S6.

lab.cmd: sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 10%  → transfer a file → capture it. Then: netem loss 100%
lab.see: ★ THE BIG ONE. At 10% loss: three duplicate ACKs, then the retransmit — FAST RETRANSMIT, live in your capture. At 100%: the RTO, and the gaps DOUBLING — 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s. Exponential backoff, on a stopwatch. Terms you name while watching them fire do not rot.

build.name: A lossy-link observatory
build.what: A proxy he routes real traffic through that DROPS, DELAYS and REORDERS packets on command — with a live view of what TCP does in response. Watch cwnd sawtooth. Watch the dup-ACKs stack up. Watch the RTO gaps double.
build.why: ★ The term `fast retransmit` is LOST and `RTO`/`exponential backoff` are WARM. He will not name them from a document — he has already proven that. He WILL name them while watching them fire.
build.real: Put it in front of a real site and break the real connection. Screenshot the sawtooth.

atoms.real: Every phone on a train. Loss spikes in a tunnel, and the connection does not die — it goes quiet and backs off. He can reproduce it exactly: `tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 10%`, then watch the retransmits.

lab.cmd: ss -ti  (in a loop, during a large transfer)
lab.see: cwnd growing — then HALVING the instant a packet drops. AIMD is not a graph in a book; it is a number on your terminal, sawtoothing.

atoms.t: UDP — and head-of-line blocking as its reason to exist. TCP: rather late than wrong. UDP: rather wrong than late
atoms.trap: Derived in S4, NEVER GATED. Covered proves nothing.
atoms.note: derived S4 from TCP's head-of-line cost. Never gated.

lab.cmd: Same 10% loss. Send a stream over TCP, then over UDP. Time both.
lab.see: TCP FREEZES — one lost packet holding ready packets hostage behind it. That freeze IS head-of-line blocking; you are watching the term. UDP keeps flowing, with holes. Rather-late vs rather-wrong, on a stopwatch.

given: head-of-line blocking (derived UDP FROM it in S4)
atoms.real: QUIC — which now carries the majority of Google's traffic and all of HTTP/3 — is built ON TOP OF UDP, on purpose, to escape TCP's head-of-line blocking. UDP is not the loser of the TCP/UDP fight. It is the foundation the winner was rebuilt on.

lacks: ★ ASYMMETRIC DIGITAL SIGNATURES — private key MAKES the mark, public key CHECKS it, neither does the other's job. HE HAS NEVER BEEN GIVEN THIS. DH is key EXCHANGE and does not imply it. This is the primitive S9 tried to interrogate out of him. HAND IT.
cryptographic hashing (sign the digest, not the document)
atoms.real: Firesheep, 2010: a one-click Firefox extension that let anyone on the same cafe wifi steal your logged-in Facebook session, because the site used HTTPS for the password page and plain HTTP for everything after. It was released PUBLICLY, on purpose, to shame the industry into TLS-everywhere. It worked.

qs.q: The attacker copies Google's cert, rips out Google's public key, drops in HIS OWN. He now needs a fresh signature at the bottom. What stops him from writing one?
qs.g: PASS — reached the right object cold: the mark can only be MADE with the CA's private key, and the attacker does not have it. Used 'mix the certificate with the CA's private key' — borrowed from the DH paint-mixing analogy. Referent correct (§1 synonym rule).

qs.q: Your laptop has to CHECK that mark. But your laptop does not have DigiCert's private key either. So what does it use to check it?
qs.g: ★ VOID — DO NOT REUSE. This question is unanswerable from what he holds. He replied 'the CA's private keys come baked into the browser' — which is wrong (it is the PUBLIC key, in a root certificate) but it is the ONLY answer available to someone who has never been given asymmetric signatures. NOT a failure of his. TEACHING_LOG Entry 010.

qs.q: You just said the attacker can't forge because he can't know the CA's private key. Now you say the private key ships in every browser — 3 billion devices. Both can't be true. Which one breaks?
qs.g: PASS (partial) — he immediately saw the contradiction ('damn then how'). BEHAVIOR_LEARNING confirmed again: he self-diagnoses reliably when shown the contradiction in HIS OWN answers. He could not resolve it, correctly, because the resolution needs the missing primitive.

beat.open: The certificate/PKI mechanism. TWO halves, and they need OPPOSITE treatment. (a) HOW the signature proves identity — needs the SIGNATURE PRIMITIVE, which he has never been given. DO NOT ASK HIM TO DERIVE IT. Derive the NEED ('you want a mark only the CA can make but anyone can check — does DH give you that?' → he says no → 'correct, so we need a new tool, here it is'), then HAND the tool. (b) WHY we trust the CA at all — this half IS derivable, because he owns trust anchor COLD from DNS root hints. Ask that one.
closed: S7: the SECRECY half — DH re-derived cold after 31 days, named unprompted.
S7: ★ the 31-day-open MITM beat — two handshakes, two keys, attacker relaying. Plus the killer line, his own: 'DH gives SECRECY, not IDENTITY'. June's CA-vs-middleman swap REPAIRED.
S9: signature-unforgeability, the MAKE half — 'only the CA's private key can make the mark'. Cold, first ask.
beat.next: Hand the signature primitive (make/check asymmetry) → he applies it to the swapped-cert case → derive WHY the CA is trusted (trust anchor, ≅ DNS root hints — he owns this) → then /lab 1.9: HE BECOMES A CA. curl REJECTED → install his own root → same curl ACCEPTED, server unchanged. Trust was never in the certificate. Then /gate 1.9.

modules.name: Foundations
modules.broke: Nothing yet — this is the floor. It was silently skipped, and that is a debt, not a choice. Every system you will ever design runs on one machine with a finite CPU, a memory hierarchy spanning six orders of magnitude, and a scheduler that can take the CPU away mid-sentence. You cannot reason about a distributed system until you can reason about one.
modules.buys: The ability to say why something is slow instead of that it is slow. Locks, races, deadlock, and the event loop — the machinery under every line of Node you have ever written.
modules.costs: Nothing breaks next. This module is the one that stops later modules from breaking. Skipping it is why isolation levels look like arbitrary SQL trivia instead of what they are — a concurrency problem in a SQL costume.

modules.name: Databases
modules.broke: You have ten servers now, and they are disposable — any one can die mid-request and be replaced by a fresh one. So where does the truth live? It cannot live in a process's memory, because processes die. That question IS a database.
modules.buys: A single place that survives a crash and can be concurrently written by many clients without them corrupting each other. That second half is the entire hard part, and it is why this module is gated on Module 0.
modules.costs: The database is now the bottleneck — one box, and every request goes through it. It also gets slow the moment it is popular. The obvious fix is to keep a copy of the hot answers somewhere fast. That is a cache, and it instantly hands you a consistency problem — because now there are two copies of the truth.

modules.name: Caching
modules.broke: The database is the bottleneck. Every request pays a disk seek for an answer that has not changed in an hour. The same question is being asked ten thousand times a second and answered from scratch every time.
modules.buys: Orders of magnitude. A RAM hit is ~100ns; a disk seek is ~100µs–10ms. That is the memory hierarchy from atom 0.1, cashed in.
modules.costs: Two copies of the truth. The instant you cache, you own an invalidation problem — and invalidation has no correct answer, only trade-offs. Then the cache itself fails in ways the DB never did: stampede, thundering herd, hot keys. And when you try to fix consistency across many caches on many machines, you find you need the machines to agree — which nobody has taught you how to do yet.

modules.name: Scalability
modules.broke: One box cannot take the load. Not the DB, not the app server, not the cache. You must add boxes — and every box you add is a new way for the system to be inconsistent, unbalanced, or on fire.
modules.buys: Boxes without chaos. Statelessness (so any box can serve any request), consistent hashing (so adding a box does not re-shuffle every key), rate limiting (so one client cannot take the system down), and the ability to estimate before you build.
modules.costs: Now failure is partial. Before, the system was up or down. Now three boxes are fine, one is slow, and — the killer — a slow machine is indistinguishable from a dead one. You cannot even tell what state your own system is in. That is the door into distributed systems, and it is the intellectual core of the whole program.

atoms.ref: Google SRE Book ch. 21–23 · Metastable Failures (HotOS'21)

modules.name: Distributed Sys
modules.broke: The machines must now agree — and there is no global clock, messages are lost, and a slow machine is indistinguishable from a dead one. You cannot ask 'is node B alive?' You can only ask 'has B replied yet?', and 'not yet' is not an answer.
modules.buys: The intellectual core of the entire program. Ordering without a clock (Lamport, vector clocks). Agreement despite failure (quorum, Raft). A precise vocabulary for what a system actually promises (the consistency lattice) instead of a marketing page's word for it.
modules.costs: Coordination is expensive and it couples. Every consensus round is a round trip; every synchronous call means if B is down, A is down. The escape is to stop calling B and instead write to a log that B reads at its own pace — which is Messaging.

atoms.t: Failure detectors — why 'is it dead?' is undecidable
Physical clocks — and why you cannot trust them
Consistency models — linearizable → sequential → causal → eventual
atoms.trap: Jepsen also documents real databases VIOLATING their own claimed guarantees. Read the analyses, not the marketing page.

atoms.ref: Raft paper + raft.github.io viz + MIT 6.824 Raft lab

atoms.t: Distributed locks — and why they are a trap

modules.name: Messaging
modules.broke: Synchronous calls couple services. If B is down, A is down. If B is slow, A is slow. If B needs to be redeployed, A takes the outage. You have built a distributed monolith with extra network hops.
modules.buys: Put a log between them. A writes to the log and leaves; B reads at its own pace; B can be down for an hour and lose nothing. The log is durable, replayable, and ordered — and that ordering is what makes it a truth rather than a buffer.
modules.costs: Everything becomes eventually consistent, and 'exactly-once' turns out to be a lie — the network cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so the best you get is at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer. That is atom 1.10 coming back to collect. Also: ordering only holds per-partition, and now you need patterns for multi-service workflows — Saga, outbox, CQRS.

atoms.trap: The LinkedIn URL is DEAD (404). Use the web.archive.org link in REFERENCES.md — every curriculum on the internet still links the dead one.

atoms.t: ⭐ The OS page cache + sendfile/zero-copy — a caught-up Kafka cluster does NO DISK READS
atoms.ref: Kafka Design docs (ties to atom 0.4, virtual memory)

atoms.trap: 'Exactly-once' is a lie without idempotency. This ties STRAIGHT back to atom 1.10 — idempotency keys.

modules.name: Storage
modules.broke: The database holds rows you query. It does not hold a 4GB video, or ten years of clickstream, or a petabyte you want to scan analytically. Different access patterns need different storage, and forcing them all into Postgres is how you get a $40k/month bill.
modules.buys: Blob storage for the big opaque things. Erasure coding for durability at a fraction of replication's cost. Columnar layout for the scans (this is your ClickHouse work, explained).
modules.costs: Now the truth is scattered across several stores with different guarantees, and keeping them coherent is its own job.

atoms.t: ⭐ Columnar storage — ties directly to your ClickHouse work

modules.name: Observability
modules.broke: You have built something you cannot see. It is 3am. It is down. Something in a graph of forty services is slow and you do not know which. What do you look at?
modules.buys: The ability to answer that question in minutes instead of hours. Metrics tell you that. Traces tell you where. Logs tell you why. And SLOs tell you whether you are even allowed to care — an error budget is permission to fail.
modules.costs: Observability is not free — cardinality explodes, tracing adds overhead, and an alert that fires too often trains you to ignore it.

atoms.t: Logging — structured, and what NOT to log
Metrics — RED (rate, errors, duration) and USE
Alerting — SLI / SLO / SLA and error budgets

modules.name: Security
modules.broke: TLS gave you a private tunnel to a server whose identity you verified. It told you nothing about who the human on the other end is, or what they are allowed to do. Atom 1.9 solved the wire. It did not solve the user.
modules.buys: AuthN (who are you) held apart from AuthZ (what may you do) — the single most-confused pair in the industry. Plus the crypto vocabulary to reason about it instead of copying a Stack Overflow answer.
modules.costs: Every mechanism here is a new attack surface. A JWT you cannot revoke. A session store that is now a bottleneck. An OAuth flow with one redirect misconfigured.

atoms.t: AuthN vs AuthZ — identity vs permission
Sessions vs JWT — the revocation problem

atoms.ref: revisits atom 1.9 — this is the DH/cert distinction, generalised

atoms.t: Hashing & salting — why a password is never encrypted
TLS in depth — revisits atom 1.9 with the full picture
CSRF / XSS / SQLi / SSRF — at a DESIGN level, not a payload level

modules.name: Infrastructure
modules.broke: You have a design. It runs on your laptop. Now put forty copies of it on machines you have never touched, replace them one at a time without dropping a request, and make it reproducible by someone who has never met you.
modules.buys: Reproducibility and safe change. A container is a machine you can diff. Blue-green and canary make a deploy reversible — which is the only thing that makes deploying often safe rather than reckless.
modules.costs: An enormous amount of accidental complexity, and an orchestrator that is itself a distributed system with its own consensus (etcd → Raft → atom 5.10).

atoms.t: Docker — and what an image actually is
Containers vs VMs — the isolation boundary

modules.name: Advanced
modules.broke: A single business action now spans five services and five databases, and there is no transaction that can span them. 2PC exists and everybody avoids it. So how do you book a flight, charge a card, and reserve a seat — atomically — when 'atomically' is not available?
modules.buys: The patterns that make multi-service correctness possible without a distributed transaction: Saga, outbox, event sourcing, CQRS. These are what senior engineers actually reach for.
modules.costs: Enormous conceptual overhead, and every one of them is eventually consistent by construction. Reach for them when you must, never because they are impressive.

atoms.t: ⭐ The outbox pattern — the fix for 'write to DB AND publish' not being atomic

modules.name: High Level Design
modules.broke: You now know every mechanism. You still cannot design a system — because designing is not recalling mechanisms, it is choosing between them under constraints you had to extract yourself, and defending the choice when someone pushes.
modules.buys: A framework that survives an hour of pressure: requirements → estimation → API → data model → architecture → scale → reliability → tradeoffs. And fifteen real designs, each of which you must defend, not recite.
modules.costs: Nothing breaks after this — but it is also the module that will most tempt you to shortcut. Grokking is deliberately NOT on this list. It teaches the shape of an answer instead of the machinery, and it rewards exactly the discriminator-dodging reflex already logged as your blind spot.

atoms.t: The framework: requirements → estimation → API → data model → architecture → scale → reliability → tradeoffs
atoms.ref: built from Modules 1–10, not from a book

modules.name: Low Level Design
modules.broke: Inside every box on your HLD diagram is code — and a beautiful architecture made of unmaintainable classes is still unmaintainable. The unit of design is COMPLEXITY, not patterns.
modules.buys: Deep modules, information hiding, and the ability to name a refactoring move instead of gesturing at it. Refactoring 2e is smell → NAME → mechanics on every page — which is an unusually good fit for a term-decay blind spot.
modules.costs: Nothing — but note the traps: Clean Code is NOT on this list (it installs rules to obey rather than a model to reason with), and GoF's patterns half-collapse into plain functions in TypeScript. Applying them as classes in Node is cargo-cult.

atoms.t: Refactoring — design as named, safe, REVERSIBLE moves
SOLID — as heuristics to RE-DERIVE, never as commandments

atoms.trap: Half of GoF (Strategy, Command, Factory Method, Template Method, Iterator) collapses into plain functions and closures in TS. Consult GoF only for its Consequences sections — the costs, which every free site amputates.

atoms.ref: ⭐ Cosmic Python (derives it from the pain it solves)

atoms.t: Fowler's EAA catalog — the vocabulary behind every ORM you touch
atoms.ref: ⭐ martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog (read the catalog, not the 2002 book)
solve COLD (ties to Module 0 — this is a semaphore)

modules.name: Interview Mastery
modules.broke: Nothing broke. This module is the byproduct, not the goal. If you can defend a design because you built the thing, this is easy. Chasing it the other way round does not work — and that is the single most common way people spend two years and get nowhere.
modules.buys: The performance layer: clarifying requirements out loud, whiteboarding legibly, articulating a tradeoff as a tradeoff rather than a preference, and STAR stories that are true.
modules.costs: Nothing. This is the last module for a reason.

atoms.t: ⭐ Tradeoff articulation — your discriminator-dodging blind spot, in its final boss form
atoms.trap: This module is where 'answering around the question' costs you the offer. It is being attacked NOW, in Module 1, on purpose.

terms.etymology: the item at the **head** of the **line** (queue) **blocks** everything behind it
terms.concept: One lost packet freezes every READY packet behind it. TCP's cost is LATENCY. This is why UDP exists.
terms.note: Derived UDP FROM it in S4 — then could not name it in S5.

terms.etymology: a **retransmit** that is **fast** — it does not wait for a timer
terms.concept: Wire FLOWING → receiver re-ACKs the last in-order byte → 3 duplicate ACKs → resend immediately.
terms.note: 'I don't know what the other mechanism is' (S5) — then re-derived it from scratch minutes later.

terms.etymology: the **time-out** that triggers a **retransmission**
terms.concept: Wire SILENT → no signal can exist → a TIMER expires → resend + exponential backoff.
terms.note: Described it perfectly; never said the name.

terms.etymology: the **same ACK**, sent **again**
terms.concept: ACKs are cumulative — 'the next byte I expect is N.' Receiving 3,4,5 while 2 is missing re-sends 'expecting 2' each time.

terms.etymology: the wait grows **exponentially** — double it each failure
terms.concept: RTO fires → resend → DOUBLE the timer → resend → double again.

terms.etymology: the attacker is **literally standing in the middle**
terms.concept: Diffie–Hellman alone shares a secret with WHOEVER IS THERE, not with WHO THEY CLAIM TO BE.
terms.note: S7: named 'man in middle' cold and pinned on the ATTACKER (right actor). The June error — calling the CA 'the middle man' — is repaired. CA and MITM now held as opposites.

terms.etymology: an **authority** that issues **certificates**
terms.concept: The trusted third party whose signature vouches for the server's identity. Pre-installed in your browser. CERT = IDENTITY. DH = SECRECY.
terms.note: S7: no longer swapped with the middleman — placed as the trusted referee. But the MECHANISM is unowned: why the signature can't be forged, why the CA is trusted (trust anchor). That is the open beat.

terms.etymology: named for its inventors — the ONE term here that really is arbitrary
terms.concept: The shared secret is BUILT INDEPENDENTLY ON BOTH ENDS and is NEVER SENT. The attacker sees both public halves and cannot un-mix them.
terms.note: Named cold unprompted at S7 open (2026-07-14) — a LATER session, so it counts (confidence rule). The mixing intuition survived 31 days; the terms were what had rotted.

terms.etymology: the **anchor** on which all **trust** rests — fixed, shipped in advance
terms.concept: Hardcoded root DNS IPs ≅ pre-installed root CAs. You must trust SOMETHING in advance to escape the 'who do I trust first?' regress.

terms.etymology: *idem* (same) + *potens* (power) → **the same effect however many times applied**
terms.concept: N runs leave the same end STATE as one run. NOT the same response.

terms.etymology: the **key** that makes a call **idempotent**
terms.concept: Client attaches a unique id; the SERVER records processed keys and returns the original result on retry. A POST tool — not a GET feature.

terms.etymology: **safe** to call — it cannot hurt anything
terms.concept: Changes NO server state at all. A pure read. GET. safe ⊂ idempotent ⊂ all.

terms.etymology: **multiplexing** = many streams into one wire · **de**-multiplexing = **splitting them back out**
terms.concept: The OS KERNEL reads the destination PORT and hands bytes to the listening process. Routers read the IP; the kernel reads the port.
terms.note: Historically fused: 'Nginx chooses the port.' It does not.

terms.etymology: it **resolves** the name, **recursively** walking the chain for you
terms.concept: The actor that DOES THE WALKING. Root/TLD/authoritative only POINT.

terms.etymology: it is the **authority** on this domain — the source of truth
terms.concept: The ONLY tier that holds the actual A record. root → TLD → authoritative.

terms.etymology: how long this record gets to **live** before it must be re-fetched
terms.concept: Bounds the cache. Past its TTL a record is STALE — not an error.

terms.etymology: old, not wrong-shaped — it **confidently points at the old address**
terms.concept: Loud failure = old server gone (timeout). QUIET failure = old server alive → you silently hit the wrong box. Quiet is more dangerous.

terms.etymology: it makes an **effort**, the **best** it can — and **promises nothing**
terms.concept: IP: packets may be lost, reordered, duplicated, corrupted, unacknowledged.

terms.etymology: **three** messages, **shaking hands** before business
terms.concept: Purpose: SYNC STARTING SEQUENCE NUMBERS, BOTH DIRECTIONS. Liveness is a side effect. Two messages confirm only one direction.

terms.etymology: a **logarithm** is just 'the exponent'; **discrete** = the integer, clock-arithmetic (mod p) version, which shatters the smooth order so there is no shortcut
terms.concept: Given g, p (public) and g^a mod p, RECOVER the secret exponent a. The hard inverse of modular exponentiation. The wall the eavesdropper cannot climb.
terms.note: S7: produced 'logarithmic' cold but dropped 'discrete' (supplied) and first aimed at the wrong object ('find g' — g is PUBLIC) before correcting the target to a. Referent right, needs one more cold pass.

terms.etymology: exponentiation, taken **modulo** p — raise g to the power then keep the remainder
terms.concept: The easy FORWARD 'mixing' direction: cheap to compute g^a mod p. Its inverse (discrete logarithm) is hopeless — that gap IS DH's secrecy.
terms.note: S7: held the 'mixing is easy' intuition cold; the term itself was supplied, not produced. Name-at-birth landed; retrieval pending.

phases.q: Two computers. No shared memory. The only way to know anything about another machine is to send a message and wait — and it may never arrive.
You skipped it. Everything above runs on ONE box with a finite CPU, a memory hierarchy spanning six orders of magnitude, and a scheduler that can take the CPU away mid-sentence.
Ten servers now, and they're disposable. Where does the truth live? That question IS a database — and the cache you reach for hands you two copies of it.
One box can't take the load. Add boxes and failure becomes PARTIAL — a slow machine is indistinguishable from a dead one. That sentence is the whole field.
You built something you cannot see, cannot deploy safely, and cannot lock down. It's 3am and it's down. What do you look at?
You know every mechanism and still cannot DESIGN. Designing is choosing under constraints you had to extract yourself — and defending it when someone pushes.

boundaries.name: The Wire
boundaries.capability: A name becomes an address (DNS). An address becomes a reliable ordered byte pipe (TCP) — which you can now BREAK and watch recover. The pipe becomes private and authenticated (TLS), and you can forge the trust yourself. And you can write all of it against raw sockets, with no framework between you and the kernel.

boundaries.name: The Edge
boundaries.capability: Everything that sits IN FRONT of an application: HTTP semantics you can defend, the three wire versions and honestly why each was built, sessions, virtual hosting, and load balancing at L4 vs L7. You can build the edge, not just call it.

boundaries.name: Real-time & APIs
boundaries.capability: Persistent bidirectional transport, typed RPC, and API contracts that survive retries, timeouts and version skew. The difference between an API that works and an API that holds under failure.
